blocks.text: If, in the face of these instructions expressed so categorically, I nevertheless refuse to carry out the Herostratic deed which my friend demands of me, I have the most cogent reasons of all for doing so.
Some of them do not admit of public discussion. Yet even those which I am able to communicate are, in my opinion, altogether sufficient for an understanding of my decision.

The principal reason: when I changed my profession in 1921, I told my friend that I had made my will, in which I asked him to destroy this and that, to look through other things, and so forth. Thereupon Kafka said, showing me from the outside the slip of paper written in ink that was later found in his writing-desk: “My will is going to be quite simple—the request to you to burn everything.” I also still remember quite distinctly the answer I gave at the time: “Should you seriously expect any such thing of me, I tell you right now that I shall not fulfill your request.” The whole conversation was conducted in that jesting tone which was customary between us, yet with the secret seriousness which each of us always presupposed in the other in doing so. Convinced of the seriousness of my refusal, Franz would have had to appoint another executor of his will if his own instruction had been a matter of unconditional and ultimate seriousness to him.

I am not grateful to him for having plunged me into this grave conflict of conscience, which he must have foreseen, for he knew the fanatical veneration I brought to every word of his, and which in the 22 years of our never-clouded friendship prompted me (among other things) not to throw away even the tiniest scrap of paper, not a single picture postcard that came from him. — Let that “I am not grateful,” by the way, not be misunderstood! What does even the gravest conflict of conscience weigh beside the infinite blessing that I owe to the friend who was the true backbone of my entire spiritual existence!

Further reasons: the order on the penciled sheet was not obeyed by Franz himself, for later on he expressly gave permission for parts of ‘Meditation’ to be reprinted in a newspaper, and for three further stories to be published, which he himself combined with “A Hunger Artist” and handed over to the publishing house Die Schmiede. Furthermore, both instructions date from a time when my friend’s self-critical tendencies had reached their peak. In the last year of his life, however, his whole existence took an unforeseen, new, happy, positive turn that abrogates this self-hatred and nihilism. — My decision to publish the literary estate is, moreover, made easier by the memory of all the bitter struggles with which I forced and often enough begged every single publication from Kafka. And yet afterward he was reconciled to these publications and relatively satisfied. — Finally, in the case of a posthumous publication a number of motives fall away, for example, that publication might unsettle further work, that it called up the shadows of personally painful periods of his life. How closely for Kafka non-publication was bound up with the problem of how he conducted his life (a problem which, to our immeasurable grief, no longer interferes now) emerges, as from many conversations, from the following letter to me: “… I am not enclosing the novels. Why stir up the old efforts? Merely because I have not burned them until now? … Next time I come, I hope it will happen. Wherein lies the sense of keeping such ‘even’ artistically unsuccessful works? In that one hopes that out of these little pieces a whole will come together, some court of appeal upon whose breast I shall be able to beat when I am in need. I know that this is not possible, that no help comes from there. So what am I to do with the things? Shall those which cannot help me harm me as well, as, given this knowledge, must be the case?”
